analogy.p: Think of a homologous series as a family in which everyone wears the same name badge, the -OH functional group. The family members (methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol) differ in height, the length of their carbon chain, so the taller family members are slower to get moving (higher boiling point), but because they all wear the same badge they all behave in the same way when something happens (they react with sodium, burn and are oxidised to acids). The analogy breaks down because real molecules are not individual people with free choice: their properties follow from the bonding and intermolecular forces, and the badge is part of the molecule, not an accessory.
analogy.t: Alcohols as a family with a name badge

bullets: Functional group: **-OH**. You must be able to recognise an alcohol from its name (ends in **-ol**) or from its formula (ends in **-OH**).
Alcohols contain only **C, H and O** and every bond is a **covalent bond**.
A homologous series has the **same functional group**, the **same general formula**, **similar chemical properties** and a **gradual trend in physical properties**.
General formula of the series: **CnH2n+1OH** (so for n = 2, C2H5OH).
Each member differs from the next by one **CH2** unit.
The -OH group is covalently bonded: alcohols are **not alkaline** and do not release OH- ions in water.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are the four members you must know by name and formula.
Link: the C=C bond makes alkenes reactive; in the same way the -OH group makes alcohols reactive.
core.h: What an alcohol is and its functional group
core.p: **Alcohols** are a **homologous series** of organic compounds whose molecules contain the **functional group -OH** (a hydroxyl group: an oxygen atom bonded to a hydrogen atom) attached to a carbon chain. A functional group is the atom or group of atoms that gives a family of compounds its characteristic chemical reactions, so every alcohol reacts in a similar way because they all contain -OH. Alcohols are made only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, all joined by **covalent bonds**, so they are small covalent molecules rather than ionic compounds. The -OH group is **not** a hydroxide ion: it is covalently bonded, which is why alcohols do not behave as alkalis.

bullets: **Methanol: CH3OH** (one carbon).
**Ethanol: C2H5OH** or CH3CH2OH (two carbons).
**Propanol: C3H7OH** or CH3CH2CH2OH (three carbons).
**Butanol: C4H9OH** or CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (four carbons).
In a displayed formula draw **H-O-C** showing the O-H bond as well as the C-O bond; a common error is to write O-H-C.
Check your drawing: every **C has four bonds**, **O has two**, **H has one**.
Molecular formula check: carbons n, hydrogens 2n+2 (including the H of the -OH), one oxygen; e.g. butanol C4H10O.
Higher tier and triple only: you are only expected to recognise alcohols, you do not need to name members beyond these four.
core.h: Names, formulae and displayed structures of the first four alcohols
core.p: The first four members are **methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol** with 1, 2, 3 and 4 carbon atoms. The stem (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) tells you the number of carbon atoms in the chain, exactly as for the alkanes, and the ending **-ol** tells you it is an alcohol. You need to be able to write the molecular formula, the structural formula and draw the displayed formula showing every atom and every bond. In a displayed formula, each carbon forms four bonds, each oxygen forms two bonds and each hydrogen forms one bond, and the O is joined to one carbon and one hydrogen.

bullets: Boiling points increase down the series: **65, 78, 97, 117 °C** (approximately) for methanol to butanol.
Reason: bigger molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces**, so **more energy** is needed to separate them; the covalent bonds inside molecules are **not** broken when they boil.
Small alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propanol) are **miscible** with water; solubility falls as the carbon chain gets longer.
Alcohols are **volatile** and **flammable**, with volatility decreasing as the chain gets longer.
Alcohols do **not conduct electricity** because they have no free ions or delocalised electrons.
Link to bonding: simple molecular substances have **low melting and boiling points** compared with ionic or giant covalent substances.
Exam link: be ready to read or draw a graph of boiling point against number of carbon atoms and describe it as a **steady increase**.
core.h: Physical properties and the trend with chain length
core.p: Alcohols are mostly liquids at room temperature, which is a surprise because small alkanes with a similar size are gases; the polar -OH group causes extra attraction between molecules. As the **chain length increases**, the molecules become larger so the **intermolecular forces** between them get stronger and more energy is needed to separate them, giving a **gradual increase in boiling point** (methanol about 65 °C, ethanol 78 °C, propanol 97 °C, butanol 117 °C). Viscosity also increases and flammability or volatility falls as the chain gets longer. This gradual change is exactly what you expect within a homologous series.

bullets: Result: a **neutral** solution, **pH 7**, universal indicator stays **green**.
Contrast: **carboxylic acids** form **weakly acidic** solutions (pH about 3 to 5, indicator orange or yellow).
Contrast: **sodium hydroxide** forms an **alkaline** solution; the OH in an alcohol is **not** a hydroxide ion.
Dissolving is a **physical change** with no new substance formed.
Ethanol is used as a **solvent** in perfumes, aftershaves and cosmetics because it dissolves many substances that water cannot.
Mark scheme phrase: **"alcohols dissolve in water to give a neutral solution"**.
Common test question: "Which pH is a solution of ethanol in water?" Answer: **7**.
core.h: Alcohols dissolve in water to form a neutral solution
core.p: Methanol, ethanol and propanol **dissolve in water** (they mix completely) and the resulting solution is **neutral**, with a pH of about 7. This is a specification fact and a very common 1 mark question. It is different from a carboxylic acid, which gives an acidic solution, and from a metal hydroxide, which gives an alkaline solution. The -OH in an alcohol does not release hydrogen ions or hydroxide ions to any significant extent, so universal indicator stays green.

bullets: Observation: **fizzing/bubbles**, the sodium **gets smaller and dissolves**; gas given off is **hydrogen**.
Test for hydrogen: lit splint gives a **squeaky pop**.
Word equation: ethanol + sodium → sodium ethoxide + hydrogen.
Symbol equation (extra detail): **2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5ONa + H2**.
The reaction is **slower and less vigorous than sodium with water**, because the O-H bond in an alcohol is less easily broken.
Safety: sodium is stored under **oil**, handled with **tongs** (never fingers), use **small pieces**, wear **eye protection**, keep away from flames because ethanol is flammable.
Higher tier link: the same reaction pattern as a **metal + acid** reaction giving hydrogen, but alcohols are **not acids**.
core.p: Alcohols **react with sodium** to produce **hydrogen gas** and a salt-like compound (a sodium alkoxide). The sodium fizzes and gradually dissolves, but the reaction is much **less vigorous** than sodium with water, so the sodium does not melt into a ball or ignite. The hydrogen can be identified with a **lit splint**, which burns with a **squeaky pop**. This reaction is a typical property of the -OH group and it is also used to show that a compound contains -OH.

bullets: Word equation: alcohol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
**Methanol: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O.**
**Ethanol: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O.**
**Propanol: 2C3H7OH + 9O2 → 6CO2 + 8H2O.**
**Butanol: C4H9OH + 6O2 → 4CO2 + 5H2O.**
How to balance: balance **C** first, then **H**, then count **O** on each side and put the remainder in front of O2.
Energy released per mole **increases** as the chain gets longer because more C and H atoms are oxidised.
Link to required practical on energy changes: burning alcohols under a **beaker or copper can of water** and using q = mc∆T to compare fuels.
core.p: Alcohols **burn in air** (they are **flammable**) and in a plentiful supply of oxygen they undergo **complete combustion** to form **carbon dioxide and water** while releasing energy as heat, so this is an **exothermic** reaction. Because alcohols already contain some oxygen in the molecule, they burn with a cleaner, **less smoky** flame than hydrocarbons of similar size. If the oxygen supply is limited, **incomplete combustion** produces carbon monoxide or carbon (soot) as well as water. The balanced equations should be written with the correct numbers.

bullets: **Fuel**: ethanol (e.g. in **gasohol/E10 petrol blends**) and methanol; burns with a clean flame.
**Solvent**: perfumes, aftershave, cosmetics, paints, inks, medical wipes, methylated spirits.
**Ethanol is the main alcohol in alcoholic drinks**: produced by fermentation of sugars in grapes, barley and other plants.
Advantage of bioethanol: **renewable**, made from crops, can be **carbon neutral** (carbon dioxide released equals carbon dioxide absorbed while growing).
Disadvantage: crops need **land**, which may compete with **food production** and cause **deforestation**; energy is used in farming, transport and distillation.
Methanol is **toxic** and ethanol is harmful in excess: alcohol misuse damages the liver and brain.
Evaluation link: Higher tier questions may ask you to compare ethanol with petrol as a fuel; mention renewable, carbon neutral, land use and cost.
core.h: Uses of alcohols: fuels and solvents
core.p: Alcohols have two main uses in the specification: as **fuels** and as **solvents**. Ethanol can be burned directly or **blended with petrol** to give **biofuel**; because it can be made by fermenting plant sugars it is described as a **renewable** fuel and, when the crops are grown, they absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, so the fuel can be **close to carbon neutral** overall. As a solvent, ethanol dissolves many substances that do not dissolve in water, which is why it is used in **perfumes, aftershaves, deodorants, cosmetics, inks and paints**. Ethanol is also the alcohol in **alcoholic drinks**.

bullets: Word equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
Symbol equation: **C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2**.
Conditions: **yeast, sugar solution, warm (about 30 to 40 °C), no oxygen (anaerobic)**.
Check the balance: 6 C, 12 H, 6 O on the left; 4 C + 2 C = 6 C, 12 H and 2 O + 4 O = 6 O on the right.
Evidence of reaction in the lab: **bubbles of carbon dioxide** through **limewater**, which turns **cloudy** (milky).
Advantages: **renewable** raw material, **low temperature**, **low energy** use, simple equipment.
Disadvantages: **slow**, **batch** process, impure and **dilute** product needing **distillation**.
Link to biology: yeast respires anaerobically, which is how bread rises and beer and wine are made.
core.p: **Fermentation** is the process that makes ethanol from **sugars** using the enzymes in **yeast**. Glucose is converted into **ethanol and carbon dioxide** by **anaerobic respiration** (without oxygen). The mixture is kept at about **30 to 40 °C**, because that is the **optimum temperature** for the yeast enzymes: too cold and the reaction is too slow, too hot and the enzymes **denature**. Fermentation is a **batch process** and it produces a **dilute** solution of ethanol (up to about 15 % before the yeast is killed by the alcohol), so **fractional distillation** is used to increase the concentration.

bullets: Equation: **C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH** (ethene + steam → ethanol).
Typical conditions: **phosphoric acid catalyst**, about **300 °C** and **60 to 70 atmospheres** (you are not usually required to recall exact values).
It is an **addition reaction** because two reactants join to form **one product only**, so the **atom economy is 100 %**.
Advantages: **fast**, **continuous** process, **pure ethanol**, high atom economy.
Disadvantages: uses **non-renewable** crude oil, high **energy** cost for high temperature and pressure.
Compare: fermentation uses **renewable** sugar and low temperature, but is **slow** and gives a **dilute** product.
Higher tier: the reaction is **reversible** (a high yield needs a compromise on conditions); unreacted ethene is **recycled**.
Link: the alkene test with bromine water shows the C=C bond that is used up in this reaction.
core.h: Making ethanol by hydration of ethene
core.p: Ethanol can also be made industrially from **ethene** (from cracking crude oil fractions) and **steam** by an **addition reaction** called **hydration**. Ethene's C=C double bond opens up and a hydrogen atom and an -OH group join the two carbon atoms. The reaction is carried out at a high temperature and pressure with a **catalyst** of phosphoric acid, and it is **reversible**, so unreacted gas is recycled to improve the yield. Because ethene is non-renewable and comes from crude oil, this method is **not sustainable** in the long term, but it gives a **pure product** and is a **fast continuous process**.

bullets: Word equation: ethanol + oxygen (from an oxidising agent) → ethanoic acid + water.
Equation using [O] for oxygen from the oxidising agent: **CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O**.
Microbial oxidation: **bacteria** in air convert ethanol in wine or beer into **ethanoic acid**, forming **vinegar**.
Lab oxidising agent: **acidified potassium dichromate(VI)**; colour change **orange to green** (extra detail; not usually asked).
Pattern: methanol → methanoic acid, ethanol → ethanoic acid, propanol → propanoic acid, butanol → butanoic acid.
The oxidation is **not** combustion: combustion would break the molecule down to CO2 and H2O.
Link to next topic: the product is a carboxylic acid with functional group **-COOH**, which is a **weak acid**.
core.h: Oxidation of alcohols to carboxylic acids
core.p: Alcohols can be **oxidised to carboxylic acids** either by reaction with an **oxidising agent** or by **microbial action** (bacteria in air). Ethanol is oxidised to **ethanoic acid**, which is why an open bottle of wine goes sour and turns to **vinegar**. In the laboratory, heating an alcohol with an acidified oxidising agent such as **potassium dichromate(VI)** converts the orange solution to green as the dichromate is reduced. In simple terms, the -CH2OH end of the molecule changes to -COOH. The oxidation of alcohols forms the link between this section and the carboxylic acids section.

bullets: **Flammable**: hazard symbol is a flame; keep away from naked flames.
**Methanol** is toxic; **methylated spirits** contains additives to discourage drinking.
Heat flammable liquids with a **hot water bath**, not directly with a Bunsen burner.
**Ethanol misuse**: damages liver, brain and slows reactions.
Risk reduction: small quantities, eye protection, good ventilation, lids on bottles.
Control measure in the sodium reaction: **small pieces** of sodium and **safety screen**.
core.p: Alcohols are **flammable** and some are **toxic**, so they must be handled carefully. **Methanol** is poisonous and can cause blindness or death if swallowed, which is why **methylated spirits** (mainly ethanol with methanol and dye added) is made undrinkable. **Ethanol** is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, but drinking too much damages the liver, brain and other organs, and it affects reaction times. In the laboratory, alcohols must be kept away from flames, and heating must be done using a **water bath** or **electric heater** rather than a naked flame.

bullets: **Alkanes**: CnH2n+2, saturated, burn, no reaction with bromine water.
**Alkenes**: CnH2n, unsaturated, decolourise **bromine water** (orange → colourless).
**Alcohols**: CnH2n+1OH, -OH, **neutral** in water, react with **sodium**, oxidised to acids.
**Carboxylic acids**: CnH2n+1COOH, -COOH, **weak acids** (pH about 3 to 5), react with carbonates giving CO2.
Test to distinguish ethanol from ethanoic acid: add **sodium carbonate** (or universal indicator); acid fizzes (CO2) and gives red/orange indicator, alcohol does not.
Test to distinguish ethanol from ethene: add **bromine water**; ethene decolourises it, ethanol does not.
Esters are formed when a **carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol** (the sweet-smelling products used in perfumes and flavourings).
Higher tier: relate properties to **structure**: -OH causes extra attraction between molecules.
core.h: Comparing alcohols with alkanes, alkenes and carboxylic acids
core.p: The **functional group** is the key to understanding organic chemistry. **Alkanes** (single C-C bonds, C-H bonds) are saturated and relatively unreactive, only burning or reacting with halogens in UV light. **Alkenes** have a C=C and undergo addition reactions. **Alcohols** have -OH and react with sodium, burn and can be oxidised. **Carboxylic acids** have -COOH, are weak acids and form esters with alcohols. Examination questions often ask you to compare series, or to give a test that distinguishes one compound from another, so learn the functional group, general formula and key reaction for each.

exam: **1 mark**: recall facts such as functional group (**-OH**), pH of an alcohol solution (**7 / neutral**), gas produced with sodium (**hydrogen**), or the name of the oxidation product (**ethanoic acid**).
**Command word 'State/Name/Give'**: a short answer is enough; do not explain unless asked.
**Command word 'Draw'**: for the displayed formula of ethanol draw every atom and every bond, including the **O-H** bond; check each C has four bonds.
**Balancing equations (2 marks)**: 1 mark for correct formulae, 1 mark for balancing: e.g. C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O.
**2 mark 'describe' question**: for fermentation write conditions: **yeast, anaerobic/no oxygen, 30 to 40 °C**; for hydration write: **ethene and steam, catalyst, high temperature and pressure**.
**'Explain why the temperature is kept at 30 to 40 °C' (2 to 3 marks)**: too low → **slow rate**/few collisions; too high → **enzymes denature** (active site changes shape), so the yeast cannot work.

**Comparison questions (4 marks)**: use **comparative words** (whereas, however, but): fermentation is renewable, low energy, slow, batch, dilute; hydration is fast, continuous, pure, but uses non-renewable ethene.

**Graph data (boiling point against carbon number)**: say 'as the number of carbon atoms increases, the boiling point increases' and quote values with units (°C); explain via **intermolecular forces**.

**6 mark 'evaluate' question**: structured answer with **advantages and disadvantages** of each method, then a **justified conclusion** (e.g. the better choice depends on whether renewable or fast/pure is more important).
**Tests**: describe the observation and the conclusion: sodium → fizzing, squeaky pop → hydrogen; bromine water → decolourises → C=C; indicator → green → neutral.
**Units**: temperature in °C, pressure in atm, energy in J or kJ; show the working in energy calculations.

mistakes.r: The functional group is -OH covalently bonded to carbon (C-O-H); alcohols are covalent molecules and the solution is neutral.
mistakes.w: Writing the alcohol group as O-H-C or as OH- ions, e.g. 'alcohols contain hydroxide ions'.

mistakes.r: Alcohols dissolve in water to give a neutral solution (pH 7).
mistakes.w: Saying alcohol solutions are alkaline because they contain OH.

mistakes.r: Alcohol + sodium produces hydrogen (squeaky pop) and sodium alkoxide, e.g. sodium ethoxide.
mistakes.w: Writing the sodium reaction gives sodium hydroxide, or that the gas is oxygen.

mistakes.r: Fermentation is anaerobic, using yeast at about 30 to 40 °C, the optimum temperature for the enzymes.
mistakes.w: Saying fermentation needs oxygen or a very high temperature.

mistakes.r: It is an addition reaction with steam: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH, one product only.
mistakes.w: Saying hydration of ethene is a substitution or gives two products.

mistakes.r: Too cold: reaction slow; too hot (above about 40 °C): enzymes denature. 30 to 40 °C gives the optimum rate.
mistakes.w: Saying the yeast is 'killed' or 'denatured' at 30 °C, or that low temperature stops it forever.

mistakes.r: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O; count the O in the alcohol itself.
mistakes.w: Unbalanced combustion equations, e.g. C2H5OH + O2 → CO2 + H2O.

mistakes.r: Oxidation of ethanol gives ethanoic acid (a carboxylic acid).
mistakes.w: Stating 'ethanol is oxidised to ethane' or 'ethene'.

mistakes.r: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
mistakes.w: Describing boiling point trend as 'the bonds get stronger'.

summary: The specification asks you to know that methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are the first four members of the alcohol homologous series with the functional group -OH, and to recognise alcohols from their names or formulae. You must know their properties (dissolve in water to give a neutral solution, react with sodium to give hydrogen, burn in air, used as fuels and solvents), that ethanol is the main alcohol in alcoholic drinks, how ethanol is made, and that alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids. It matters because alcohols are a key link between alkenes, carboxylic acids and esters in organic chemistry.

terms.d: A member of the homologous series of organic compounds containing the -OH functional group, with general formula CnH2n+1OH.
The atom or group of atoms in a compound that determines its characteristic chemical reactions.
A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties.
The -OH functional group, an oxygen atom covalently bonded to a hydrogen atom.
The conversion of sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide by the enzymes in yeast, in anaerobic conditions at about 30 to 40 °C.
An addition reaction in which water (steam) adds across a double bond; ethene + steam → ethanol.
A reaction in which two or more reactants join to form a single product, with no other products.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen (or loses electrons); alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids.
A homologous series with the -COOH functional group, formed by oxidation of alcohols.
Able to mix completely with another liquid in all proportions to give one layer.
A liquid that dissolves a solute to form a solution.
A fuel made from plant or animal material, such as ethanol made by fermenting sugar crops.
A separation technique using differences in boiling point; used to concentrate ethanol from a fermentation mixture.
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water only.
Having a pH of 7, neither acidic nor alkaline.

worked.q: Ethanol burns completely in oxygen: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O. Relative atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 4.6 g of ethanol burns completely. (4 marks)
steps: Moles of ethanol = mass ÷ Mr = 4.6 ÷ 46 = **0.10 mol**.
From the equation 1 mol of ethanol gives **2 mol** of CO2, so moles CO2 = 0.10 × 2 = **0.20 mol**.

worked.q: Fermentation of glucose: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that can be made from 90 g of glucose. (Mr glucose = 180, Mr ethanol = 46.) (3 marks)
steps: Equation ratio: 1 mol glucose gives 2 mol ethanol, so moles ethanol = 0.50 × 2 = **1.0 mol**.
Mass of ethanol = moles × Mr = 1.0 × 46 = **46 g**.

worked.ans: Model answer: Fermentation uses renewable sugar, yeast and a low temperature (30 to 40 °C) with no oxygen, but is slow, batch and gives dilute ethanol that needs distilling. Hydration uses ethene from non-renewable crude oil with steam, a catalyst, high temperature and pressure, but it is fast, continuous and gives pure ethanol with 100 % atom economy.
worked.q: Compare the production of ethanol by fermentation with its production by hydration of ethene. (4 marks)
steps: Fermentation uses **sugar from plants**, a **renewable** raw material, whereas hydration uses **ethene from crude oil**, which is **non-renewable**.
Fermentation uses **yeast** at about **30 to 40 °C** without oxygen, whereas hydration uses **steam, a phosphoric acid catalyst, high temperature and high pressure**.
Fermentation is a **slow batch process** giving a **dilute** product needing distillation, whereas hydration is **fast and continuous** and gives **pure** ethanol.
Hydration is an addition reaction with **100 % atom economy**, while fermentation also makes carbon dioxide as a by-product.
